title: Lecture 3: Central Bank and Monetary Policy

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Hey everyone, Maya here.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Leo here. And today, the central bank. Lecture three. Central Bank and Monetary Policy in China.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Which, I'll be honest, is the densest one so far. So we're going to focus on the story and the big ideas, and leave the tables for the summary tab.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Deal. So, start simple. What does a central bank do?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The classic list. It issues the only legal currency. It's the bankers' bank, meaning the lender of last resort when banks are in trouble. It's the government's bank and runs the payment system. It conducts monetary policy. And it supervises.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the PBOC does all that, plus more.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Plus two extra jobs. It manages the exchange rate, and it administers the capital account, meaning the rules on money flowing in and out of China. And the slide says those aren't side duties. They're the reason its toolbox has to be so big.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And it's not independent like the Fed.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. It's a ministry level body under the State Council. Its legal mandate is, quote, maintain the stability of the value of the currency, and thereby promote economic growth. And the Central Financial Commission, the Party body, sets the direction.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: How big is it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Its balance sheet is about forty two trillion yuan, one of the biggest central bank balance sheets in the world. And inside it, you have SAFE, the digital yuan institute, the cross border payment system, the credit registry.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, and then there's the history. Seven stages. Let's do it like a story.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Okay. Stage one, nineteen forty eight to seventy eight. The monobank. The PBOC is founded on December first, nineteen forty eight, in Shijiazhuang, from merging three banks. And for thirty years it's basically the only bank. Its job is to match credit to the production plan.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the slide says that wasn't stupid.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. The line is, a coherent framework matched to planning, not a crude precursor. If prices aren't set by markets, interest rate tools wouldn't work anyway.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Stage two, the split.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Nineteen seventy nine to eighty four. Four state banks split off, and the loan for grant reform. State firms stop getting free budget money and start getting bank loans instead. In nineteen eighty four, ICBC is carved out to take over the PBOC's commercial lending.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the key line there?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The split created the banks. It did not yet create banking.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Ooh. Because they're still just lending where the plan tells them.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. They're cashier windows, not credit risk judges. Stage three. Inflation. Two of them. In nineteen eighty eight, price reform pushes inflation to around eighteen percent. Then in the early nineties, there's a credit surge, and by nineteen ninety four inflation peaks around twenty four percent.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Twenty four percent!

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah. And a big part of the problem was that local PBOC branches were lending to local projects under pressure from local governments.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So the local branch manager gets a call from the governor saying, we need this factory, lend the money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Basically. So in nineteen ninety three, there's a big decision on financial reform. Create a real central bank, separate policy banks from commercial banks, centralize monetary policy. And the key line: the second inflation, not the first, produced the legal framework.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Stage four, nineteen ninety five, the PBOC Law.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And there's one line in it that the lecture calls the one line that made it a central bank. Article twenty nine. No overdraft to the government. No direct purchase of treasury debt.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So the government can't just print money to pay its bills.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. And the slide argues that's the real independence. Not who appoints the governor, but the ban on directly financing the deficit.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: But there's a twist.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There's a twist. After two thousand eight, local governments found a workaround. They created local government financing vehicles, LGFVs, which borrowed from banks, not from the PBOC. So the rule held, but the financing just moved off budget.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Classic. Okay, stage five.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Nineteen ninety eight. To stop local capture, they abolished provincial branches and created nine regional branches that crossed province lines. So no single governor controlled a branch. And credit quotas were abolished. Big moment.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And that lasted until...

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Twenty twenty three, when they went back to provincial branches. Times change, digital systems, different problems. Stage six, two thousand three. Bank supervision gets moved out into a separate regulator, the CBRC. So the PBOC focuses on monetary policy.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: But that created gaps.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Right. The central bank sees the big picture, the regulator sees individual banks, and things fall between them. Like shadow banking. And stage seven, since twenty seventeen, coordination. Committees, mergers of regulators, and eventually the NFRA in twenty twenty three. That's actually the whole next lecture.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the big lesson from all seven stages?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Reform is crisis driven, not scheduled. Separate functions when the conflict gets costly, coordinate again when the separation gets costly. Back and forth.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Alright. Money. M zero, M one, M two.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: M zero is cash. Notes and coins. About twelve trillion yuan. The only thing the PBOC fully controls. M one adds demand deposits, money in checking accounts that you can spend right away. And M two adds savings and time deposits. About three hundred thirteen trillion.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And there's this scissors gap thing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah, this is nice. If M one grows faster than M two, money is being activated. People and firms are moving money into spending accounts, so the economy is heating up. If M two grows faster, money is being parked in savings. People are cautious.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And M one was redefined recently.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: December twenty twenty four. The old M one only counted corporate checking accounts. But with mobile payments, so much spending money sits in personal accounts and in Alipay or WeChat Pay reserves. The old M one actually fell for eighteen months while retail sales were growing. So they added household demand deposits and payment institution reserves.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, and the M two to GDP ratio. China's is like, huge?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: About two hundred thirty two percent. The US is around seventy two.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Why?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Because the system is bank based. Savings sit as deposits instead of in stocks or funds. High savings rate, about forty five percent. Few other places to put money, except housing. And deposit rates are kept low, so banks have lots of cheap funding.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Does that mean inflation?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not automatically. It's more a sign that each unit of capital produces less GDP over time. And it stopped rising after twenty seventeen, when shadow banking was reined in.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, the balance sheet. Three eras.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: This is one of my favorite slides, because it tells the whole story through the balance sheet. Era one, two thousand three to twenty fourteen. China is exporting like crazy. Exporters earn dollars, swap them for yuan at banks, banks swap them with the PBOC. So the PBOC is buying dollars and creating yuan. Foreign assets go up to about twenty seven trillion yuan.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And that's a lot of new money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Way too much. So they have to sterilize it. Soak it back up. They issue central bank bills and they raise the reserve requirement, the RRR. That's the share of deposits banks must park at the central bank.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: How high did that go?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: From about six percent in two thousand three to about twenty one percent by twenty eleven.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Twenty one percent of deposits, just locked up. Wow.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The slide calls it quantity absorbing quantity. Era two, twenty fifteen to twenty nineteen. The dollars stop flowing in. So now the PBOC injects money differently, by lending to banks. Tools like the MLF, the medium term lending facility, and the PSL, pledged supplementary lending for policy banks.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And era three, the twenty twenties, structural tools.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Targeted lending to specific sectors. Green, tech, small firms, rental housing. And the takeaway: money creation now depends on the PBOC's lending decisions, not the trade surplus.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, monetary policy itself. Objectives, instruments, transmission.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Objectives first. The Fed has a dual mandate, prices and jobs. The ECB has basically one, inflation. The PBOC pursues several at once. Price stability, growth, employment, balance of payments, financial stability. With no published ranking.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Which sounds flexible, but also kind of confusing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The lecture says exactly that. Pragmatic for a developing economy, but it creates target conflicts and makes it less transparent.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, and then the phases of policy. What's the moment where modern Chinese monetary policy is born?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Nineteen ninety eight. When credit quotas are abolished. Before that, the PBOC literally told banks how much to lend. After that, it manages overall liquidity instead.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And twenty fifteen is another turning point.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Three things in one year. In August, the eight eleven FX reform, the daily fixing becomes more market based and the yuan drops about three percent in one go. Capital starts flowing out. Second, the stock market crash, the Shanghai index falls about forty five percent. And third, the interest rate corridor gets formalized.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Explain the corridor, because I always get confused.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Think of a hallway. The ceiling is the rate banks pay for emergency borrowing from the central bank. That's the SLF. Nobody would borrow from each other above that, they'd just go to the central bank. The floor is the rate the central bank pays on excess reserves, IOER, point three five percent. Nobody lends below that, they'd just leave the money at the central bank.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And the market rate bounces around in between.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly, the overnight interbank repo rate, DR zero zero one. And in the middle you have the policy rate, the one the PBOC actually steers. That was the seven day reverse repo from July twenty twenty four. And very recent news on the slides: since November second, twenty twenty six, the anchor moved to the overnight reverse repo at one point two five percent.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So that's like, this month.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yeah, literally a few weeks ago. Worth remembering for the exam.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Then the LPR reform in twenty nineteen.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The problem was, the PBOC would cut rates and corporate borrowing costs barely moved, because banks priced loans off an old benchmark. So in twenty nineteen they fixed the loan prime rate, the LPR, which twenty banks quote every month, and tied it to the policy rate. Now it's policy rate, then LPR, then your loan rate.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: The last mile.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Almost. The slide says the real last mile is deposit rates, which are still coordinated, not competed.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And then why is the price channel weak overall?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Four links. Policy rate, deposit rate, lending rate, real activity. And each leaks. Deposit rates are sticky. Lending rates get negotiated with state linked borrowers. And the big one, borrowers with implicit guarantees don't care about price.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: The soft budget constraint again!

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's everywhere. If you know you'll be bailed out, a rate hike doesn't scare you. So the slide says it's an institutional problem, not a technical one. That's why quantity tools stuck around.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay, last piece. The impossible trinity.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: You can only have two out of three. Independent monetary policy, a fixed exchange rate, and free capital flows. China, from ninety four to twenty fifteen, kept monetary independence and a managed exchange rate, and gave up free capital flows. Capital controls.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: So the reserve pile and the high RRR were the cost of keeping the currency stable.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Exactly. And after twenty fifteen, more flexibility in the exchange rate, but controls still there. And when fighting deflation means cutting rates, which weakens the currency, China uses the capital account to handle that, not the interest rate.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Okay. Three things to remember?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: One. The PBOC does more jobs than the Fed or the ECB, including the exchange rate and the capital account, and it pursues several objectives at once. Two. Its history is crisis driven. The second inflation gave us the nineteen ninety five law, and Article twenty nine, no direct financing of the government, is its real independence. And three. China's toolbox is long because the price channel is weak, mainly because of soft budget constraints. The big reforms, ninety eight abolishing credit quotas, the corridor, the twenty nineteen LPR reform, are all about making the price channel work.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: And next time, regulators. Even more acronyms.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Oh, so many. See you then.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Bye!
